3   I.    FACTS                                                          
4         In the past decade, rapid technological development has shaped and reshaped 
5   commerce.  Artificial  intelligence  is  now  disrupting  industries  throughout  the  world 
6   economy. The ways that people shop, consume entertainment, move about, and vacation 
7   have fundamentally changed. So, too, has the way that people conduct major transactions 
8   such as home selling and buying.                                     
9        iBuying, short for instant buying, is a relatively recent phenomenon intended to 
10   simplify  major  transactions.  (Doc.  39  ¶¶ 51,  52.)  Powered  by  advanced  technology, 
11   iBuyers, or businesses engaged in iBuying, use automated valuation models to price homes. 
12   (Id. ¶ 51.) Based on those valuations, iBuyers attempt to quickly purchase and resell 
13   homes. (Id.)                                                         
14        Founded in 2014, Opendoor is an iBuying company operating in the residential real 
15   estate market. (Id.  ¶¶ 51-52.)  Its  process  follows the typical structure of an iBuying 
16   business. Individuals looking to sell their homes can go to Opendoor’s website or mobile 
17   app, input some relevant data points, and receive an “instant” cash offer generated by 
18   Opendoor’s proprietary algorithm. (Id. ¶ 53.) After making the initial offer, Opendoor 
19   personnel conduct a virtual assessment and adjust the offer based on the home’s condition. 
20   (Id.) Then, Opendoor makes a final offer, which is reduced by a 5% service charge. (Id.) If 
21   the homeowner accepts, Opendoor pays the seller, takes ownership of the home, makes 
22   repairs if necessary, and lists it for resale. (Id. ¶¶ 55, 75-76.)   
23        Opendoor’s algorithm is central to the success of its iBuying business. (Id. ¶¶ 56, 
24   59.) To consistently sell homes at a profit, Opendoor’s algorithm must produce generally 
25   accurate initial offers. (Id. ¶ 4.) While those initial offers will often be adjusted after the 
26   homes’ unique defects are revealed through an inspection, they must provide Opendoor 
27   with a viable starting point. (Id. ¶¶ 4, 53.) Accordingly, the algorithm must account for the 
28   value of the homes at the time of the initial offer and accurately forecast their future value. 
1   (Id. ¶¶ 4, 7, 60.) The algorithm purports to do this by relying on frequently expanding, 
2   comprehensive sets of hyperlocal data. (Id. ¶ 58.) It uses that data, according to Opendoor, 
3   to anticipate market changes and thereby generate offers reflective of a home’s true  
4   value—not just today, but in the future. (Id. ¶¶ 7-9.)               
5        Opendoor has worked toward this objective since its inception. (Id. ¶¶ 3, 52, 56.) It 
6   began as a private company, but in 2020, went public via a reverse merger with Defendant 
7   Social Capital Hedosophia Holdings Corp. II, a Special Purpose Acquisition Company 
8   (“SPAC”).2 (Id. ¶ 324.) After the de-SPAC merger, the surviving entity changed its name 
9   to Opendoor Technologies Inc. (Id. ¶ 325.) Then, in December of that year, Opendoor 
10   published offering documents which registered the first issuance of shares of Opendoor 
11   common stock. (Id.) On December 21, 2020, the newly issued Opendoor shares began 
12   publicly trading on the NASDAQ stock exchange. (Id.) In February 2021, Opendoor 
13   published new offering documents registering the issuance of additional stock. (Id. ¶ 327.) 
14   On February 9, 2021, those shares began publicly trading. (Id.)      
15        As Opendoor informed stockholders, its iBuying business is its main revenue driver. 
16   (Id. ¶ 55.) In evaluating the financial health of that business, Opendoor told its investors 
17   that “[t]he ultimate measure [they] should hold [Opendoor] accountable for is how [it is] 
18   doing on contribution margin delivery.” (Id. ¶ 8.) Contribution margin refers to a metric 
19   used “to understand how a specific product contributes to [a] company’s profit.” Amy 
20   Gallo, Contribution Margin: What It Is, How to Calculate It, and Why You Need It, Harvard 
21   Business Review (Oct. 13, 2017), https://hbr.org/2017/10/contribution-margin-what-it-is-
22   how-to-calculate-it-and-why-you-need-it.  In  this  case,  the  “product”  is  Opendoor’s 
23   iBuying operation.

7        Lead Plaintiffs are retirement service providers that purchased Opendoor stock on

11   throughout the Class Period. (Doc. 39-3.) Together, Plaintiffs allege that Defendants made 
12   several materially misleading statements during the Class Period, that those statements 
13   artificially inflated Opendoor’s stock price, that they relied on those statements, and that 
14   they suffered damages when the stock price dropped after the truth was revealed. (See 
15   generally Doc. 39.)                                                  
16        Against the Opendoor Defendants, Plaintiffs assert claims under Section 10(b), 15 
17   U.S.C. § 78j(b) and Section 20(a), 15 U.S.C. § 78t(a) of the Exchange Act of 1934, and

19   (Id. ¶¶ 305-19, 480-99.) Against the Underwriter Defendants, they assert one claim under 
20   Section 11. (Id. ¶¶ 480-92.) Defendants responded by filing their Motions to Dismiss. 
21   (Docs. 48, 51.)                                                      
22   II.   LEGAL STANDARD                                                 
23        To survive a motion to dismiss pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6), “a complaint 
24   must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to ‘state a claim to relief that is 
25   plausible on its face.’” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (quoting Bell Atl. Corp. 
26   v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007)). A claim is facially plausible when it contains 
27                                                                        
    3 Lead Plaintiffs are Indiana Public Retirement System, Oakland County Employees’ 
28   Retirement System, and Oakland County Voluntary Employees’ Beneficiary Association. 
    (Doc. 20.)                                                           
1   “factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference” that the moving 
2   party is liable. Id. At the pleading stage, the Court’s duty is to accept all well-pleaded 
3   complaint allegations as true. Id. Facts should be viewed “in the light most favorable to the 
4   non-moving party.” Faulkner v. ADT Sec. Servs., Inc., 706 F.3d 1017, 1019 (9th Cir. 2013). 
5   “[D]ismissal . . . is proper if there is a lack of a cognizable legal theory or the absence of 
6   sufficient facts alleged under a cognizable legal theory.” Conservation Force v. Salazar, 
7   646 F.3d 1240, 1241-42 (9th Cir. 2011) (internal marks omitted).     
8        Securities fraud suits face heightened pleading standards. “At the pleading stage, a 
9   complaint stating claims under [S]ection 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 must satisfy the dual 
10   pleading requirements of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 9(b) and the PSLRA.” Zucco 
11   Partners, LLC v. Digimarc Corp., 552 F.3d 981, 990 (9th Cir. 2009).  
12             Because allegations of fraud inescapably carry a degree of 
              moral  turpitude,  Rule  9(b)  imparts  a  heightened  note  of 
13                                                                        
              seriousness,  requiring  a  greater  degree  of  pre-discovery 
14             investigation  by  the  plaintiff,  followed  by  the  plaintiff’s 
              required  particular  allegations,  thereby  protecting  a 
15                                                                        
              defendant’s  reputation  from  frivolous  and  unfounded   
16             allegations  and  permitting  a  particularized  basis  for  a 
              defendant to respond to the particularized allegations.    
17                                                                        
18   Irving Firemen’s Relief & Ret. Fund v. Uber Techs., Inc., 998 F.3d 397, 404 (9th Cir. 2021) 
19   (citation omitted).                                                  
20        Similarly, the PSLRA requires that “the complaint shall specify each statement 
21   alleged to have been misleading, the reason or reasons why the statement is misleading, 
22   and, if an allegation regarding the statement or omission is made on information and belief, 
23   the complaint shall state with particularity all facts on which that belief is formed.” 15 
24   U.S.C. § 78u-4(b)(1)(B). The PSLRA “prevents a plaintiff from skirting dismissal by filing 
25   a complaint laden with vague allegations of deception unaccompanied by a particularized 
26   explanation stating why the defendant’s alleged statements or omissions are deceitful.” 
27   Metzler Inv. GMBH v. Corinthian Colls., Inc., 540 F.3d 1049, 1061 (9th Cir. 2008) 
28   (emphasis in original).                                              
1   III.   DISCUSSION                                                    
2        A.   Section 10(b)                                              
3        “Section 10(b) of the Exchange Act prohibits manipulative or deceptive practices in 
4   connection with the purchase or sale of a security.” In re Facebook, Inc. Sec. Litig., 87 
5   F.4th 934, 947 (9th Cir. 2023) (internal marks omitted). Rule 10b-5 of the Exchange Act’s 
6   implementing regulations, which is coextensive with Section 10(b), “prohibits making ‘any 
7   untrue statement of a material fact’ or omitting material facts ‘necessary in order to make 
8   the statements made, in the light of the circumstances under which they were made, not 
9   misleading.’” Id. (quoting Glazer Cap. Mgmt., L.P. v. Forescout Techs., Inc., 63 F.4th 747, 
10   764 (9th Cir. 2023) (quoting 17 C.F.R. § 240.10b-5(b))).             
11        To state a claim under Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5, a plaintiff must sufficiently 
12   allege: “(1) a material misrepresentation or  omission; (2) made with scienter; (3) in 
13   connection with the purchase or sale of a security; (4) reliance on the misrepresentation or 
14   omission; (5) economic loss; and (6) loss causation.” In re BofI Holding Sec. Litig., 977 
15   F.3d 781, 786 (9th Cir. 2020). Each of these elements must be independently satisfied. See 
16   Or. Pub. Emps. Ret. Fund v. Apollo Grp. Inc., 774 F.3d 598, 607 (9th Cir. 2014) (reasoning 
17   that failure to adequately plead an element constitutes “an independent basis” on which to 
18   affirm dismissal of a securities fraud complaint). As explored below, Plaintiffs successfully 
19   pleads six misrepresentations attributable to the Opendoor Defendants. Nonetheless, they 
20   fail to meet their pleading standards as to scienter and loss causation.  
21             1.   Actionable False or Misleading Statements             
22        The Opendoor Defendants first argue that Plaintiffs’ Section 10(b) claim fails 
23   because Plaintiffs have not alleged that they made any actionable false or misleading 
24   statements. (Doc. 48 at 18-28; Doc. 60 at 7-18.) In response, Plaintiffs point to several 
25   categories of statements made by the Opendoor Defendants alleged in the Consolidated 
26   Amended Complaint to have been false or misleading. (Doc. 56 at 15-21.) 
27        “A plaintiff can allege falsity by ‘point[ing] to [the] defendant’s statements that 
28   directly contradict what the defendant knew at the time.” Jaeger v. Zillow Grp., Inc., 644 
1   F. Supp. 3d 857, 870 (W.D. Wash. 2022) (quoting Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc., 
2   899 F.3d 988, 1008 (9th Cir. 2018)). “[A] statement is misleading if it would give a 
3   reasonable investor the ‘impression of a state of affairs that differs in a material way from 
4   the one that actually exists.’” Berson v. Applied Signal Tech., Inc., 527 F.3d 982, 985 (9th 
5   Cir. 2008) (quoting Brody v. Transitional Hosps. Corp., 280 F.3d 997, 1006 (9th Cir. 
6   2002)). “To be misleading, a statement must be ‘capable of objective verification.’” Retail 
7   Wholesale & Dep’t Store Union Local 338 Ret. Fund v. Hewlett-Packard Co., 845 F.3d 
8   1268, 1275 (9th Cir. 2017) (quoting Or. Pub. Emps. Ret. Fund, 774 F.3d at 606).  
9                  i.   Statements Regarding the Pricing Algorithm       
10        Plaintiffs allege that the Opendoor Defendants, through their challenged statements, 
11   “created  the  impression  that  [Opendoor’s]  success  was  the  result  of  its  AI-powered 
12   algorithm, which they claimed drove pricing decisions and kept Opendoor profitable in any 
13   housing market by reacting to changing economic conditions.” (Doc. 55 at 15.) Plaintiffs 
14   challenge the following statements regarding the accuracy and operability of Opendoor’s 
15   pricing algorithm:                                                   
16     •  The algorithm uses “machine learning to drive pricing decisions.” (Doc. 39 ¶ 169.) 
17     •  Opendoor’s  “proprietary,  machine  learning-based  pricing  models  are  key  to 
18        [Opendoor’s] ability to acquire and resell thousands of homes per month accurately, 
19        profitably, and with increasing levels of automation.” (Id. ¶ 173.) 
20     •  The algorithm can “dynamically adjust to leading market indicators and react to 
21        real-time macro- and micro-economic conditions.” (Id. ¶¶ 169, 177.) 
22     •  The algorithm’s ability to “dynamically price homes in response to both micro and 
23        macro factors [] allows [Opendoor] to manage . . . within [a] 4% to 6%, annual 
24        [contribution] margin range, [] regardless of the home cycle [Opendoor is] operating 
25        in.” (Id. ¶ 186.)                                               
26   (Doc. 55 at 15.)                                                     
27        Plaintiffs allege that these statements were misleading because “the algorithm could 
28   not accurately price homes (even in a hot market) and as such [Opendoor’s] pricing 
1   decisions were based on a human-driven process that led to [Opendoor’s] success.” (Id. at 
2   9.) This fact has been confirmed, say Plaintiffs, by several former employees. (Doc. 
3   39 ¶¶ 62-73.) For example, “[a]ccording to CW 5, who was brought in to price initial 
4   offers, approximately 50% of the properties were sent to human pricing analysts for 
5   review.” (Doc. 55 at 16 (citing Doc. 39 ¶ 71).) Additionally, “CW 2 stated that her 
6   managers continuously told pricing analysts to not even use the algorithm to generate final 
7   offers because the algorithm was never accurate and would corrupt the pricing analysts’ 
8   assessment of market value.” (Id. (citing Doc. 39 ¶¶ 63-64).) Plaintiffs also point to 
9   findings made by the Federal Trade Commission (“FTC”) in 2019 as further evidence that 
10   people did the work publicly attributed to Opendoor’s algorithm. (Id.) 
11        The Opendoor Defendants counter that Plaintiffs’ allegations conflate their business 
12   practices in the initial and final offer stages. (Doc. 48 at 20-21 n.11.) They argue that 
13   Opendoor never claimed that all its pricing decisions were driven by its algorithm. (Id. at 
14   20-21.) Instead, Opendoor’s initial offers were driven primarily (though not entirely) by its 
15   algorithm, but creating final offers required the aid of substantial human involvement. This 
16   makes sense. While the pricing algorithm took the lead in generating an initial offer based 
17   on available data, that initial offer had to be adjusted by the unique characteristics that each 
18   individual  property  possessed—such  as  damaged  or  aged  aspects  that  may  have 
19   necessitated repairs. This latter task naturally required personal intervention.  
20        The Opendoor Defendants say that they disclosed the existence of this human 
21   involvement in the following statements:4                            
22     •  “The majority of our initial offers are algorithmically generated and do not require 
23        any human intervention.” (Doc. 49-1 at 45.)                     
24

2        finalized  by  members  of  our  pricing  team,  allowing  us  to  marry  the  best  of 
3        algorithmic insights with human judgment.” (Doc. 49-2 at 10.)

7        really good job of integrating systematic modeling with [] the human insight and the

9   (Doc. 48 at 20-21.)                                                  
10        The  Opendoor  Defendants  also  argue  that  Plaintiffs’  confidential  witnesses 
11   corroborate the disclosures. (Doc. 60 at 10.) For example, CW 2’s statement that about 
12   90% of final offers were generated by pricing analysts is consistent with Opendoor’s 
13   disclosure that its final offers come after human adjustments. CW 5’s estimate that about 
14   50% of initial offers were reviewed by humans is generally consistent with Opendoor’s 
15   disclosure that most, though not all, of its initial offers do not involve human intervention.   
16        Plaintiffs, however, contend that the Opendoor Defendants’ disclosures fall short 
17   because they do not “disclose[] that Opendoor was forced to rely on humans to price its 
18   offers because its algorithm could not accurately price homes . . . [or] that [Opendoor] was 
19   engaged in deceptive practices . . . that contributed to [Opendoor’s] profitability.” (Doc. 55 
20   at 17.) Additionally, Plaintiffs argue that the “[t]he instant case is strikingly analogous to 
21   the securities fraud lawsuit against Zillow [in Jaeger, 644 F. Supp. 3d 857], which investors 
22   brought after Zillow left the iBuying business in November 2021.” (Id.) In both cases, say 
23   Plaintiffs,  the  companies  relied  on  extensive  human  involvement  in  their  pricing 
24   scheme while  misleading  investors  into  believing  that  their  algorithms  drove  their 
25   success. (Id. at 18.)                                                
26        Plaintiffs’ arguments are unavailing. First, Jaeger is distinguishable. There, Zillow 
27   sought to rapidly scale up its iBuying operation in an attempt to catch up to its competitors. 
28   Jaeger, 644 F. Supp. 3d at 865-66. To do so, Zillow devised a plan that it called “Project 
1   Ketchup.” Id. In Project Ketchup, Zillow “applied systematic overlays to drive up offers 
2   well above the pricing indicated by its algorithm and pricing analysts.” Id. at 866 (internal 
3   marks omitted). Put another way, Zillow purposefully raised its offer prices well beyond 
4   those generated by its algorithm. See id. Publicly, Zillow presented a different picture to 
5   investors and led them to believe that it was actively relying on its algorithm. Id. Instead, 
6   under Project Ketchup, Zillow was raising the offers generated by its algorithm in an 
7   attempt to purchase more homes more quickly, thereby increasing its market share. Id. 
8   Thus, Zillow’s statements were misleading. Id.                       
9        Plaintiffs’ attempt to frame Opendoor’s conduct in a similar light is unconvincing. 
10   They allege that, like Zillow, Opendoor concealed its practices of adjusting initial offers in 
11   the final offer stage and failing to refund deductions made for anticipated repairs that 
12   became unnecessary. (Doc. 39 ¶¶ 170-74; Doc. 55 at 18.) But unlike Project Ketchup, 
13   those practices  were  sufficiently  disclosed  to  investors  and  consistent  with  the 
14   Opendoor Defendants’ public statements. (Doc. 49-1 at 10, 45; Doc. 49-2 at 10, 11, 19; 
15   Doc. 49-3 at 10.)                                                    
16        The Court also finds that, even taking the facts in the light most favorable to 
17   Plaintiffs, the four challenged statements are not false and would not have misled a 
18   reasonable  investor.  The  Opendoor  Defendants’  statement  that  the  algorithm  used 
19   “machine learning to drive pricing decisions” is a simple statement about Opendoor’s use 
20   of AI in its pricing scheme and does not suggest that Opendoor personnel lack any 
21   significant role in that process. Nor does the Opendoor Defendants’ representation that 
22   Opendoor’s  algorithm  is  “key”  to  the  success  of  its  business  model.  The  other  two 
23   challenged  statements—about  the  algorithm’s  ability  to  dynamically  adjust  and  keep 
24   Opendoor  within  a  4%  to  6%  annual  contribution  margin—likewise  would  not  lead 
25   reasonable investors to conclude that Opendoor’s entire process, from initial offer to final 
26   offer,  was  driven  by  its  algorithm.  This  is  especially  true  in  light  of  the  Opendoor 
27   Defendants’ disclosures. As discussed below, however, Plaintiffs successfully pleaded 
28   these two latter statements as misleading insofar as they suggest that Opendoor’s algorithm 
1   was accurately estimating and forecasting home values.               
2                  ii.  Statements Regarding Profitability               
3        Plaintiffs next argue that the Opendoor Defendants misled investors by guaranteeing 
4   Opendoor’s “ability to remain profitable in any housing market.” (Doc. 55 at 19.) Plaintiffs 
5   challenge the following statements:                                  
6     •  The algorithm can “dynamically adjust to leading market indicators and react to 
7        real-time macro- and micro-economic conditions.” (Doc. 39 ¶¶ 169, 177.) 
8     •  “[O]ur model really works in upmarkets, it’s going to work in flat markets, it’s going 
9        to work in downmarkets.” (Id. ¶ 181 (spelling in original).)    
10     •  The algorithm’s ability to “dynamically price homes in response to both micro and 
11        macro factors [] allows [Opendoor] to manage . . . within [a] 4% to 6%, annual 
12        [contribution] margin range, [] regardless of the home cycle [Opendoor is] operating 
13        in.” (Id. ¶ 186.)                                               
14     •  “[I]f you run the business model through the worst recession in U.S. history, we 
15        would still have positive contribution margin.” (Id. ¶ 189.)    
16     •  Opendoor “ha[s] good evidence that [it] can operate in [a] declining market.” 
17        (Id. ¶ 192.)                                                    
18     •  Opendoor’s “systems are doing exactly what they’re designed to do, which is 
19        responding very quickly, adjusting prices to market.” (Id. ¶ 199.) 
20   (Doc. 55 at 15, 19-20, 23.)                                          
21        According to Plaintiffs, “the algorithm never worked as Defendants claimed.” (Doc. 
22   55 at 20.) And, according to Plaintiffs, many of the same confidential witness statements 
23   cited above support this contention. (Supra at 8; see also Doc. 39 ¶¶ 62-73; Doc. 55 at 22.)  
24        The Opendoor Defendants argue that the challenged statements are not misleading 
25   because their many disclaimers notified reasonable investors that the algorithm could not 
26   guarantee profitability. (Doc. 48 at 19-20.) They cite the following statements from the 
27   Opendoor Defendants as disclosing the risk that Opendoor could incur losses: 
28     •  “Our  business  is  dependent  upon  our  ability  to  accurately  price  and  portfolio 
1        manage inventory and an ineffective pricing or portfolio management strategy may 
2        have a material adverse effect on our business.” (Doc. 49-1 at 10-11.)  
3     •  Opendoor  could  “incur  significant  losses  in  the  future”  due  to  its  “failure  to 
4        appropriately price and manage the home inventory [it] acquire[d].” (Doc. 49-2 
5        at 17.)                                                         
6     •  Opendoor “may be unable to liquidate . . . inventory at prices that allow [it] to meet 
7        [its] margin targets or recover [its] costs.” (Doc. 49-1 at 11.)  
8     •  Opendoor’s  “success  depends,  directly  and  indirectly,  on  general  economic 
9        conditions, [and] the health of the U.S. residential real estate industry, particularly 
10        the single family home resale market.” (Id. at 7-8.)            
11     •  “Home  prices  can  be  volatile  and  the  values  of  [Opendoor’s]  inventory  may 
12        fluctuate significantly.” (Id. at 14.)                          
13     •  “Mortgage rates are currently low as compared to most historical periods,” and rate 
14        increases “could result in a decline in the demand for [Opendoor’s] homes” and 
15        “adversely affect [Opendoor’s] business or financial results.” (Id. at 15-16.) 
16     •  “[C]hanging  market  conditions  are  reflected  in  [Opendoor’s]  pricing  for  new 
17        acquisitions,  largely  leaving  previously  acquired  inventory  at  risk  to  potential 
18        market volatility.” (Doc. 49-2 at 12.)                          
19   (Doc. 48 at 13, 19-20.)                                              
20        Plaintiffs  argue  that  the  Opendoor  Defendants’  disclosures  were  insufficient 
21   because (1) they did not correct the impression that the algorithm “worked in all housing 
22   markets;” and (2) they did not disclose that the algorithm already failed to accurately 
23   estimate home value. (Doc. 55 at 21-22.) The first argument can be quickly dismissed. It 
24   stands to reason that no reasonable investor would ever believe that a particular business 
25   model, even one premised on impressive technology, is guaranteed to be profitable in all 
26   circumstances.                                                       
27        Plaintiffs also rely on statements from financial analysts writing for Wedbush, 
28   InvestorPlace, and Seeking Alpha to argue that reasonable investors believed Opendoor’s 
1   algorithm  to  guarantee  profitability.  (Doc.  39 ¶¶ 96-99.)  Based  on  the  Opendoor 
2   Defendants’ allegedly misleading statements and financial success, those writers reported 
3   favorably on Opendoor’s algorithm. (Id.) But none of the statements, as recited in the 
4   Consolidated  Amended  Complaint,  evidence  a  belief  that  Opendoor’s  algorithm  was 
5   guaranteed to accurately price and forecast home values in every housing market; instead, 
6   they indicate general enthusiasm that Opendoor’s algorithm was “best in class” and the 
7   “best in the business.” (Id.) The Court cannot equate such statements with an endorsement 
8   that a particular technology is perfect or unfailing.                
9        The statements do, however, reflect an impression that Opendoor’s algorithm was, 
10   at the very least, generating roughly accurate initial offers at the time the statements were 
11   made. If the algorithm was in fact already failing to accurately estimate home values, the 
12   analysts cited in the Consolidated Amended Complaint were incorrect in their impressions. 
13   Plaintiffs adequately allege that the analysts’ erroneous  conclusions were  due to the 
14   Opendoor Defendants’ purportedly misleading statements regarding the efficacy of their 
15   algorithm. (Id. ¶¶ 96-99, 112.) Because “[t]he perceptions of analysts are an acceptable 
16   measure of what reasonable investors would have understood,” Jaeger, 644 F. Supp. 3d. at 
17   872, the Court finds that, taking Plaintiffs’ allegations as true, a reasonable investor would 
18   have been misled by the Opendoor Defendants’ statements into believing that Opendoor’s 
19   algorithm  was  accurately  estimating  and  forecasting  home  values  at  the  time  the 
20   statements were made.                                                
21        The Opendoor Defendants argue that their misleading statements are nonetheless 
22   non-actionable puffery. (Doc. 48 at 24-27.) “In the Ninth Circuit, vague, generalized 
23   assertions of corporate optimism or statements of mere puffing are not actionable material 
24   misrepresentations under federal securities laws because no reasonable investor would rely 
25   on such statements.” In re Restoration Robotics, Inc. Sec. Litig., 417 F. Supp. 3d 1242, 
26   1255  (N.D.  Cal.  2019)  (internal  quotations  and  citations  omitted).  “When  valuing 
27   corporations, . . . investors  do  not  rely  on  vague  statements  of  optimism  like  ‘good,’ 
28   ‘well-regarded,’ or other feel good monikers.” In re Cutera Sec. Litig., 610 F.3d 1103, 
1   1111 (9th Cir. 2010); see also In re Verifone Sec. Litig., 784 F. Supp. 1471, 1481 (N.D. 
2   Cal. 1992) (“Professional investors, and most amateur investors as well, know how to 
3   devalue the optimism of corporate executives, who have a personal stake in the future 
4   success of the company.”). Far from being a guarantee of unshakable financial success, the 
5   statements, according to the Opendoor Defendants, expressed justified corporate optimism 
6   of the type that courts routinely deem non-actionable puffery. (Doc. 48 at 26-27.)  
7        The Court finds that the Opendoor Defendants’ statements are too concrete and 
8   verifiable to constitute non-actionable puffery. See e.g., Jaeger, 644 F. Supp. 3d at 872-73. 
9   Each  of  the  challenged  statements  are  premised  on  a  concrete,  verifiable            
10   supposition—Opendoor’s algorithm, at a bare minimum,  can accurately estimate and 
11   forecast home values. Opendoor’s algorithm either does this in up, flat, and down markets 
12   or it does not. In the face of rapid economic downturn, it either responds very quickly and 
13   adjusts prices to market or it does not. It is either capable of keeping Opendoor within a 
14   4% to 6% contribution margin range or it is not. These elements of concreteness and 
15   verifiability were not present in the cases relied upon by the Opendoor Defendants. See 
16   Plevy v. Haggerty, 38 F. Supp. 2d 816, 827-28 (C.D. Cal. 1998); Hutton v. McDaniel, 264 
17   F. Supp. 3d 997, 1021 (D. Ariz. 2017); Macomb Cnty. Emps.’ Ret. Sys. v. Align Tech., Inc., 
18   39 F.4th 1092, 1099 (9th Cir. 2022).                                 
19        Thus, the Court finds that these six challenged statements are actionably misleading 
20   because they would have led a reasonable investor to conclude that Opendoor’s algorithm 
21   was  accurately  pricing  homes  and  adjusting  to  changes  within  the  market  when  the 
22   statements were made.                                                
23                  iii.  Statements Regarding Opendoor’s Business Model and the 
24                       2019 FTC Complaint                               
25        Plaintiffs  next  argue  that  the  Opendoor  Defendants  misled  investors  by 
26   mischaracterizing  its  business  model. (Doc. 55 at 23-24.)  The  Opendoor Defendants 
27   claimed  that  Opendoor’s  “business  model  is  designed  to  generate  margins  from 
28   [Opendoor’s] service charge to sellers and ancillary products and services associated with 
1   a transaction, and not from the spread between acquisition price and resale price.” (Doc. 
2   39 ¶ 175.) Plaintiffs argue that Opendoor’s business model more heavily relied upon gains 
3   from reselling houses. They point to a 2019 FTC complaint against Opendoor charging that 
4   “gains  from  selling  homes  for  more  than  its  offer  price  are  a  key  contributor  to 
5   [Opendoor’s] revenue.” (Id. ¶ 150 (quoting Doc. 49-7) (alteration in original).)  
6        The Opendoor Defendants reply that investors were fully aware that Opendoor 
7   generated revenue from reselling homes. (Doc. 48 at 25; Doc. 60 at 17 nn.10, 13-14.) 
8   Specifically, Opendoor told investors that it “aim[ed] to maximize resale margin.” (Doc. 
9   49-1 at 45; see also Doc. 49-25 at 54, 62.) Because Opendoor adequately disclosed that it 
10   sought to resell homes at a profit, the Court finds that, even taking Plaintiffs’ allegations 
11   as true, a reasonable investor would not have been misled by the challenged statement. 
12        Plaintiffs next allege that the Opendoor Defendants misled investors by reassuring 
13   them that “the allegations raised by the FTC are related to activity that occurred between 
14   2017 and 2019.” (Doc. 39 ¶ 196.) In fact, say Plaintiffs, the activity continued throughout 
15   the Class Period. But Plaintiffs do not allege that the conduct giving rise to the FTC 
16   complaint—allegedly misleading advertising practices—continued. (See generally Doc. 
17   39;  see  also  Doc.  49-7.)  Instead,  they  allege,  based  on  the  detailed  statements  of 
18   confidential  witnesses,  that  Opendoor  personnel  continued  to  manually  adjust  the 
19   algorithm’s offers and charge sellers for repairs that they did not make. (Id. ¶¶ 62-84, 
20   143-49.) But Opendoor repeatedly disclosed that people had a role in pricing and that repair 
21   credits were estimates for which Opendoor bore the risk or reward of staying within budget. 
22   (See e.g., Doc. 49-2 at 10, 11.) Therefore, the Court finds that a reasonable investor would 
23   not have been misled by this challenged statement.                   
24             2.   Scienter                                              
25        To state a claim under Section 10(b), Plaintiffs must make a showing of scienter, 
26   i.e., an intent to defraud. See Ernst & Ernst v. Hochfelder, 425 U.S. 185, 193 (1976) 
27   (explaining  that  scienter  refers  to  the  mental  state  embracing  an  “intent  to  deceive, 
28   manipulate, or defraud”). “Mere negligence—even head-scratching mistakes—does not 
1   amount to fraud.” Prodanova v. H.C. Wainwright & Co., LLC, 993 F.3d 1097, 1103 
2   (9th Cir. 2021).                                                     
3        Rule  9(b),  moreover,  requires  a  plaintiff  to  “state  with  particularity  the 
4   circumstances constituting fraud.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b). In enacting the PSLRA, Congress 
5   extended Rule 9(b)’s particularity requirement to allegations of scienter. Therefore, to 
6   adequately plead scienter, a complaint must “state with particularity facts giving rise to a 
7   strong inference that the defendant acted with the required state of mind.” 15 U.S.C. 
8   § 78u-4(b)(2)(A). To support a strong inference of scienter, a complaint must allege that a 
9   defendant made false or misleading statements with an “intent to deceive, manipulate, or 
10   defraud,” or with deliberate recklessness. City of Dearborn Heights Act 345 Police & Fire 
11   Ret. Sys. v. Align Tech., Inc., 856 F.3d 605, 619 (9th Cir. 2017). “Deliberate recklessness 
12   is not mere recklessness.” Prodanova, 993 F.3d at 1106 (internal marks and citation 
13   omitted) (emphasis in original). Rather, it is “an extreme departure from the standards of 
14   ordinary care . . . which presents a danger of misleading buyers or sellers that is [] known 
15   to the defendant or is so obvious that the actor must have been aware of it.” Id. (emphasis 
16   in original).                                                        
17        These  standards  “present  no  small  hurdle  for  the  securities  fraud  plaintiff.” 
18   Schueneman v. Arena Pharms., Inc., 840 F.3d 698, 705 (9th Cir. 2016) (citation omitted); 
19   see also Nguyen v. Endologix, Inc., 962 F.3d 405, 414 (9th Cir. 2020) (“The PSLRA’s 
20   strong inference requirement has teeth. It is an exacting pleading obligation.”) (cleaned 
21   up). The Court must “engage in a comparative evaluation [and] . . . consider, not only 
22   inferences urged by the plaintiff . . . but also competing inferences rationally drawn from 
23   the facts alleged.” Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights Ltd., 551 U.S. 308, 314 (2007).  
24   A complaint will survive a motion to dismiss “only if a reasonable person would deem the 
25   inference of scienter cogent and at least as compelling as any opposing inference one could 
26   draw from the facts alleged.” Id. at 324.                            
27        The Opendoor Defendants argue that Plaintiffs have failed to adequately plead 
28   scienter. (Doc. 48 at 28-34; Doc. 60 at 18-23.) Plaintiffs disagree. (Doc. 55 at 25-32.) They 
1   respond that the Consolidated Amended Complaint adequately pleads scienter through five 
2   different avenues. (Id.) But as explained below, the Court finds to the contrary. 
3                  i.   Defendant Wu’s Stock Sales                       
4        Defendant Wu is a co-founder of Opendoor, the former Chairman of Opendoor’s 
5   Board of Directors, and Opendoor’s former Chief Executive Officer. (Doc. 39 ¶ 39.) 
6   Plaintiffs argue that his sale of a portion of his Opendoor stock is “highly indicative of 
7   scienter.” (Doc. 55 at 26; Doc. 39 ¶¶ 239-47.) Setting aside the question of whether a single 
8   defendant’s  trading  can  establish  a  strong  inference  of  scienter  for  a  group  of 
9   co-defendants, the Court finds that Defendant Wu’s sales do not even establish a strong 
10   inference of scienter as to him.                                     
11         “‘To evaluate suspiciousness of stock stales, [the Court] consider[s], inter alia, 
12   three factors: (1) the amount and percentage of shares sold; (2) timing of the sales; and (3) 
13   consistency with prior trading history.’” In re Quality Sys., Inc. Sec. Litig., 865 F.3d 1130, 
14   1146 (9th Cir. 2017) (quoting Nursing Home Pension Fund, Loc. 144 v. Oracle Corp., 380 
15   F.3d 1226, 1232 (9th Cir. 2004)).                                    
16        First, the amount and percentage of shares sold by Defendant Wu do not indicate 
17   scienter. Plaintiffs allege that, between November 16 and 18, 2021, Defendant Wu sold 7% 
18   of his Opendoor stock. (Doc. 39 ¶ 239; see also Doc. 55 at 29.) They concede that this is a 
19   relatively small percentage but argue that “even sales of a relatively small percentage of an 
20   insider’s holdings can support an inference of scienter if the absolute dollar value of the 
21   transactions is high.” (Doc. 55 at 29.) For example, Plaintiffs rely upon In re SeeBeyond 
22   Technologies  Corp.  Securities  Litigation,  266  F.  Supp.  2d  1150  (C.D.  Cal.  2003) 
23   (hereinafter “In re SeeBeyond”). But In re SeeBeyond is readily distinguishable, as the 
24   court’s decision relied on the fact that the “defendants . . . admittedly lied to analysts and 
25   investors.” 266 F. Supp. 2d at 1169. Not so here. Additionally, the Court finds that courts 
26   within  the  Ninth  Circuit  routinely  find  that  sales  of  similarly  small  percentages  of 
27   defendants’ stock holdings do not give rise to a strong inference of scienter. See e.g., In re 
28   Alteryx, Inc. Sec. Litig., No. 8:20-cv-01540 DOC (JDEx), 2021 WL 4551201, at *4 (C.D. 
1   Cal. June 17, 2021); Zamir v. Bridgepoint Educ., Inc., No. 15-CV-408 JLS (DHB), 2016 
2   WL 3971400, at *10 (S.D. Cal. July 25, 2016); In re Juniper Networks, Inc., 158 F. App’x 
3   899, 901 (9th Cir. 2005).                                            
4        Nor  does  the  timing  of  Defendant  Wu’s  sales  indicate  scienter.  The  parties 
5   characterize those sales somewhat differently. As told by Plaintiffs, Defendant Wu’s sales 
6   were suspiciously timed because they were made outside the parameters of his 10b5-1 plan 
7   and  came  just  three  days  after  he  provided  allegedly  false  reassurances  to  investors 
8   following Zillow’s exit from the iBuying marketplace.5 (Doc. 55 at 26-27.) But according 
9   to the Opendoor Defendants, Defendant Wu had no traditional 10b5-1 plan at all. (Doc. 60 
10   at 20-21.) Instead, his sales were pre-determined and exclusively intended to cover tax 
11   liability. (Id.) Zillow’s exit is irrelevant because that was not due to the failure of its 
12   algorithm, but its plan to overprice homes in order to gain market share. (Id. at 21.) Finally, 
13   Defendant Wu’s one-year lockup period under SEC Rule 144 had just expired, leaving him 
14   free to unload stock; thus, such rapid sales are not unusual.6 (Id.) 
15        Plaintiffs’ allegations fail to meet the exacting pleading standards imposed by Rule 
16   9(b) and the PSLRA. A reasonable person would not deem the inference of scienter “cogent 
17   and at least as compelling as [the] opposing inference” that Defendant Wu’s sales were due 
18   to the expiration of his lockup period. See Tellabs, 551 U.S. at 314. Moreover, Defendant 
19   Wu’s Opendoor stock holdings actually increased during the Class Period. (Doc. 48 at 29; 
20   Doc. 60 at 19.) Plaintiff discounts this fact as irrelevant because Defendant Wu’s stock 
21   acquisitions “were part of his compensation and thus do not undercut an inference of 
22   scienter.” (Doc. 55 at 29.) But this Court has previously found that “net gain[s] of shares 
23   during  the  class  period  cuts  against”  a  plaintiff’s  theory  that  stock  sales  support  an 
24   inference  of  scienter.  City  of  Pontiac  Gen.  Emps.  Ret.  Sys.  v.  First  Solar  Inc.,  No.

27   and    Exchange   Commission   (last  visited  Feb.   7,    2024),   
    https://www.sec.gov/reportspubs/investor-publications/investorpubsrule144.  The  rule

1   CV-22-00036-PHX-MTL, 2023 WL 155861, at *8 (D. Ariz. Jan. 10, 2023). 
2        Neither  party  addresses  the  third  factor—whether  Defendant  Wu’s  sales  were 
3   consistent with his prior trading history. (See Doc. 48 at 28-31; Doc. 55 at 26-29; Doc. 60 
4   at 18-21.) The Consolidated Amended Complaint alleges only that the sales “were by far 
5   Defendant Wu’s largest sales of Opendoor stock historically.” (Doc. 39 ¶ 244.) But it does 
6   not provide any “meaningful trading history for purposes of comparison to the stock sales

8        Accordingly, the Court finds that Plaintiffs’ allegations concerning Defendant Wu’s 
9   stock sales fail to support a strong inference of scienter.          
10                  ii.   Core Operations Doctrine                        
11        Plaintiffs next attempt to plead scienter through the “core operations” doctrine. 
12   (Doc. 39 ¶¶ 248-53.) This theory “relies on the principle that corporate officers have 
13   knowledge of the critical core operation of their companies.” Police Ret. Sys. of St. Louis 
14   v. Intuitive Surgical, Inc., 759 F.3d 1051, 1062 (9th Cir. 2014) (internal marks omitted). 
15   Core operations may support a strong inference of scienter under three circumstances:  
16                                                                        
              First, the allegations may be used in any form along with other 
17             allegations  that,  when  read  together,  raise  an  inference  of 
              scienter that is cogent and compelling, thus strong in light of 
18             other  explanations  .  .  .  .  Second,  such  allegations  may 
19             independently satisfy the PSLRA where they are particular and 
              suggest  that  defendants  had  actual  access  to  the  disputed 
20             information . . . . Finally, such allegations may conceivably 
21             satisfy the PSLRA standard  in a more  bare form,  without 
              accompanying particularized allegations, in rare circumstances 
22             where the nature of the relevant fact is of such prominence that 
              it would be absurd to suggest that management was without  
23                                                                        
              knowledge of the matter.                                   
24                                                                        
25   S. Ferry LP, No. 2 v. Killinger, 542 F.3d 776, 785-86 (9th Cir. 2008) (internal marks 
26   omitted). “Proof under this theory is not easy.” Intuitive Surgical, Inc., 759 F.3d at 1062. 
27   To successfully allege scienter under the core operations doctrine, “[a] plaintiff must 
28   produce  either  specific  admissions  by  one  or  more  corporate  executives  of  detailed 
1   involvement  in  the  minutia  of  a  company’s  operations  .  .  .  or  witness  accounts 
2   demonstrating that executives had actual involvement in creating false reports.” Id.  
3        Plaintiffs’  arguments  regarding  the  core  operations  doctrine  are  brief  and 
4   ambiguous. (See Doc. 39 ¶¶ 248-53.) For example, Plaintiffs state that “it is implausible to 
5   suggest that Defendants did not know about the human-driven process for pricing.” (Doc. 
6   55 at 30 (cleaned up).) But they also state, much more broadly, that “‘it would be absurd 
7   to suggest that management was without knowledge of’ the algorithm’s true capabilities.” 
8   (Id. (quoting Reese v. Malone, 747 F.3d 557, 577 (9th Cir. 2014).) In either case, the 
9   Consolidated Amended Complaint lacks the necessary particularized allegations to plead 
10   scienter through the core operations doctrine.                       
11        While the Consolidated Amended Complaint adequately alleges that the algorithm 
12   was the core of Opendoor’s operations, Plaintiffs have not “produce[d] either specific 
13   admissions by one or more corporate executives of detailed involvement in the minutia of 
14   [Opendoor’s pricing] operations . . . or witness accounts demonstrating that executives had 
15   actual involvement in creating false reports.” Intuitive Surgical, Inc., 759 F.3d at 1062. In 
16   the  Consolidated  Amended  Complaint,  Plaintiffs  generally  assert  that  because  the 
17   algorithm was so crucial to the success of the business, the Opendoor Defendants must 
18   have been aware of the algorithm’s efficacy. (See Doc. 39 ¶¶ 248-53.) In their response 
19   brief, Plaintiffs additionally argue that the 2019 FTC investigation into Opendoor must 
20   have made the Opendoor Defendants aware of the algorithm’s present inability to estimate 
21   and forecast home values accurately. (Doc. 55 at 30.)                
22        The Court finds that Plaintiffs’ allegations are insufficient to establish a strong 
23   inference of scienter through the core operations doctrine. First, their vague allegations 
24   based on the algorithm’s general importance are insufficient. See Palm Harbor Special 
25   Fire Control & Rescue Dist. Firefighters Pension Plan v. First Solar Inc., No. CV-22-
26   00036-PHX-MTL, 2023 WL 4161355, at *5 (D. Ariz. June 23, 2023) (“Although Plaintiffs 
27   argue that it ‘would be absurd to suggest that Defendants were not aware of the problems 
28   with the Series 6 module[,]’ the law requires more in the form of specific admissions or 
1   witness accounts.”). Similarly, Plaintiffs’ reliance on the FTC investigation is misplaced. 
2   The FTC investigation had nothing to do with the accuracy of Opendoor’s algorithm. (See 
3   generally Doc. 49-7.) Thus, the core operations doctrine is no help to Plaintiffs.  
4                  iii.   Zillow’s Exit from the iBuying Marketplace     
5        Plaintiffs also argue that Zillow’s exit from the iBuying marketplace supports an 
6   inference of scienter. (Doc. 39 ¶¶ 273-75; Doc. 55 at 30-31.) They say that because Zillow 
7   was a major competitor, presumably with expansive resources, but nonetheless exited the 
8   iBuying space “because of its failure to accurately price homes” (Doc. 39 ¶ 273), the 
9   Opendoor Defendants “knew, or were reckless in not knowing, that their algorithm was not 
10   able to accurately price homes in any environment” (id. ¶ 274).      
11        The Court is unpersuaded. Plaintiffs merely insinuate that, following Zillow’s exit, 
12   the  Opendoor Defendants  either did or should have concluded that if Zillow cannot 
13   succeed, they cannot either. But Plaintiffs’ allegations fail to specify with the level of 
14   particularity demanded by the PSLRA why the Court should assume that Zillow’s failure 
15   justifies an inference that the Opendoor Defendants were aware of their own algorithm’s 
16   alleged shortcomings or were reckless in failing to discover those shortcomings. (See Doc. 
17   39 ¶¶ 273-75.) Nor do Plaintiffs refer the Court to any case where a similar inference was

23   Amended] Complaint alleges was withheld from investors” and because “Opendoor had 
24   conducted internal analyses showing its employees manually adjusted offers and charged

26   undisclosed practices. (Doc. 55 at 31.) While the FTC investigation dealt with alleged

1        As the Court finds in this Order, the Opendoor Defendants’ statements concerning 
2   the role of people in its pricing scheme and the nature of its repair estimates were not false 
3   or  misleading.  (Supra  at  7-11.)  As  to  the  statements  the  Court  does  find            
4   misleading—dealing with the algorithm’s efficacy—the FTC investigation is irrelevant. It 
5   sheds no light on whether Opendoor’s algorithm was accurately estimating and forecasting 
6   home values at the time the misleading statements were made. (See generally Doc. 49-7.) 
7   As a result, the FTC investigation is not evidence that the Opendoor Defendants were aware

10                  v.   The Opendoor Defendants’ Statements              
11        Plaintiffs finally argue that the Opendoor Defendants’ statements regarding the 
12   algorithm’s capabilities, references to internal testing of the algorithm, and timing of their 
13   statements support an inference of scienter. (Doc. 39 ¶¶ 108, 181, 254-63; Doc. 55 at 31.) 
14   But again, the Consolidated Amended Complaint lacks particularized allegations that the 
15   Opendoor  Defendants  possessed  contradictory  information  about  the  efficacy  of  the 
16   algorithm. (See generally Doc. 39 ¶¶ 254-63.) For example, Plaintiffs do not specifically 
17   allege that Opendoor’s internal testing revealed that the algorithm was not accurately 
18   estimating or forecasting home values. (See generally id.) Nor do they allege that such 
19   troubling test results, if indeed they existed, were conveyed to the Opendoor Defendants.

22        Accordingly, the Court finds that Plaintiffs’ allegations do not meet the demanding 
23   requirements imposed by Rule 9(b) and the PSLRA. They are insufficient to establish a

25   brought pursuant to Section 10(b) fail.                              
26             3.   Loss Causation                                        
27        Even if Plaintiffs had adequately pleaded a strong inference of scienter, their Section 
28   10(b) claims against the Opendoor Defendants would still fail due to their failure to plead 
1   loss causation.                                                      
2        Section 10(b) requires that plaintiffs asserting securities fraud “must plead and 
3   ultimately prove that the defendant’s wrongful conduct caused the plaintiff’s injury.” In re 
4   BofI Holding, 977 F.3d at 789. In enacting the PSLRA, Congress codified the requirement 
5   that plaintiffs “shall have the burden of proving that the act or omission of the defendant 
6   alleged to violate [the law] caused the loss for  which the plaintiff seeks to recover 
7   damages.” 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(b)(4).                                   
8        “Typically, to establish loss causation, a plaintiff must show that the defendants’ 
9   alleged misstatements artificially inflated the price of stock and that, once the market 
10   learned of the deception, the value of the stock declined.” Irving Firemen’s Relief & Ret. 
11   Fund, 998 F.3d at 407 (citing Nuveen Mun. High Income Opportunity Fund v. City of 
12   Alameda,  Cal.,  730  F.3d  1111,  1119-20  (9th  Cir.  2013)).  This  is  known  as  the 
13   “fraud-on-the-market” theory. Nuveen, 730 F.3d at 1120. To advance this theory, “the 
14   plaintiff must show that after purchasing her shares and before selling, the following 
15   occurred: (1) the truth became known, and (2) the revelation caused the fraud-induced 
16   inflation in the stock’s price to be reduced or eliminated.” In re BofI Holding, 977 F.3d at 
17   789 (internal marks omitted). “The most common way for plaintiffs to prove that ‘the truth 
18   became known’ is to identify one or more corrective disclosures.” Id. at 790 (citing 
19   Mineworkers’ Pension Scheme v. First Solar Inc., 881 F.3d 750, 753-54 (9th Cir. 2018) 
20   (per  curiam)).  Corrective  disclosures  occur  “when  ‘information  correcting  the 
21   misstatement or omission that is the basis for the action is disseminated to the market.’” Id. 
22   (quoting 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(e)(1)).                                   
23        While  determining  what  constitutes  a  corrective  disclosure  “has  proved  more 
24   challenging than might have been expected, a few basic ground rules can be sketched out.” 
25   Id. at 790. Corrective disclosures do not require “an admission of fraud by the defendant 
26   or a formal finding of fraud by a government agency.” Id. (citing Metzler, 540 F.3d at 
27   1064).  Rather,  a  corrective  disclosure  can  “come  from  any  source,  including 
28   knowledgeable third parties such as whistleblowers, analysts, or investigative reporters.” 
1   Id. (citation omitted). Also, corrective disclosures “need not reveal the full scope of the 
2   defendant’s  fraud  in  one  fell  swoop;  the  true  facts  concealed  by  the  defendant’s 
3   misstatements may be revealed over time through a series of partial disclosures.” Id. 
4   (citation omitted). While corrective disclosures “need not precisely mirror the earlier 
5   misrepresentation, [they] must at least relate back to the misrepresentation and not to some 
6   other negative information about the company.” Grigsby v. BofI Holding, Inc., 979 F.3d 
7   1198, 1207-08 (9th Cir. 2020) (quoting Lloyd v. CVB Fin. Corp., 811 F.3d 1200, 1210

15   underwriters,  and  so  forth)  for  material  misstatements  or  omissions  in  registration

17   U.S. 175, 179 (2015). The text of the statute provides in relevant part: 
18

19             became effective, contained an untrue statement of a material

20             therein  or  necessary  to  make  the  statements  therein  not 
21             misleading,  any    person    acquiring  such              
              security . . . may . . . sue.

23   15 U.S.C. § 77k(a). Section 11 therefore “creates two ways to hold issuers liable for the 
24   contents of a registration statement—one focusing on what the statement says and the other 
25   on what it leaves out.” Omnicare, Inc., 575 U.S. at 179.             
26        To  prevail  on  a  Section  11  claim,  a  plaintiff  must  demonstrate  that  (1) “the 
27   registration statement contained an omission or misrepresentation,” and (2) “the omission 
28   or misrepresentation was material, that is, it would have misled a reasonable investor about 
1   the nature of his or her investment.” In re Daou Sys., Inc., 411 F.3d 1006, 1027 (9th Cir. 
2   2005) (quoting In re Stac Elecs. Sec. Litig., 89 F.3d 1399, 1403-04 (9th Cir. 1996)). 
3   Scienter is not required for liability under Section 11. Id. A defendant is “liable for innocent 
4   or negligent material misstatements or omissions.” Id.               
5        1.   Applicability of Rule 9(b)’s Heightened Pleading Standard  
6        Importantly, “the heightened pleading requirements of the PSLRA do not apply to 
7   Section 11 claims.” Rubke v. Capitol Bancorp Ltd., 551 F.3d 1156, 1161 (9th Cir. 2009). 
8   Nonetheless, “plaintiffs are required to allege their claims with increased particularity 
9   under Rule 9(b) if their complaint sounds in fraud.” Id. (cleaned up). The Ninth Circuit has 
10   advised that where “a complaint employs the exact same factual allegations to allege 
11   violations of [S]ection 11 as it used to allege fraudulent conduct under [S]ection 10(b) of 
12   the Exchange Act, [the Court] can assume that it sounds in fraud.” Id. Otherwise, the Court 
13   must consider “whether the complaint ‘allege[s] a unified course of fraudulent conduct’ 
14   and rel[ies] entirely on that course of conduct as the basis of a claim.” Id. (quoting Vess v. 
15   Ciba-Geigy Corp. USA, 317 F.3d 1097, 1103-04 (9th Cir. 2003)) (alterations in original). 
16   If it does, the claim sounds in fraud. Id.                           
17        The parties disagree over whether Rule 9(b) applies to Plaintiffs’ Section 11 claims. 
18   The Opendoor Defendants argue that it does because the claims sound in fraud. They argue 
19   that “although Plaintiffs expressly disclaim that their Section 11 claim sounds in fraud, this 
20   disclaimer is belied by their repeating of the exact same factual allegations used to support 
21   their Section 10(b) claim.” (Doc. 48 at 18 (cleaned up).) The Underwriter Defendants join 
22   in the Opendoor Defendants’ arguments. (Doc. 51 at 8-9; Doc. 62 at 7-9.)  
23        Plaintiffs counter that their Section 11 claims do not sound in fraud because “the 
24   [Consolidated  Amended]  Complaint  carefully  segregates  Plaintiffs’  negligence-based 
25   Securities Act claims from the fraud-based Exchange Act claims,” “the Securities Act 
26   claims expressly disclaim any allegations of fraud, fraudulent conduct, improper motive or 
27   any intentional or reckless misconduct,” and “the Securities Act and Exchange Act claims 
28   are distinct claims against different defendants.” (Doc. 56 at 13-14 (cleaned up).) 
1        The Court finds that Plaintiffs’ Section 11 claims sound in fraud because the exact 
2   same factual allegations underlie both Plaintiffs’ Sections 10(b) and 11 claims. (Compare 
3   Doc. 39 ¶¶ 62-84, 118-29, 166-82 with id. ¶¶ 401-60.) Specifically, Plaintiffs allege the 
4   exact same false or misleading statements. (Compare id. ¶¶ 169, 173, 175, 177 with 
5   id. ¶¶ 402, 405, 407, 410, 412, 414.) Because “the [S]ection 11 claim . . . merely relies on 
6   the same alleged misrepresentations . . . that are central to Plaintiff[s]’ [S]ection 10(b) fraud 
7   claim . . . Plaintiff[s]’ [S]ection 11 claim is grounded in fraud and must meet Rule 9(b)’s 
8   pleading requirements.”  In re Rigel Pharms., Inc. Sec.  Litig., 697 F.3d 869, 885-86 
9   (9th Cir. 2012) (hereinafter “In re Rigel”).                         
10        Plaintiffs’  disclaimer  does  not,  on  its  own,  evade  Rule  9(b).  Knollenberg  v. 
11   Harmonic,  Inc.,  152  F.  App’x  674,  684  (9th  Cir.  2005)  (“[A]  disclaimer  alone  is 
12   insufficient to re-characterize a complaint whose gravamen is plainly fraud . . .”); See also 
13   In re Rigel, 697 F.3d at 885-86. There is no magic pleading technique that transforms a 
14   claim otherwise based in fraud into one that is not. Knollenberg, 152 F. App’x at 684; see 
15   also In re Rigel, 697 F.3d at 885-86. Instead, Plaintiffs’ reliance on the same false or 
16   misleading statements alleged in its Section 10(b) claim controls the outcome. In re Rigel, 
17   697 F.3d at 885-86. Finally, and for the same reasons, the fact that the claims are not 
18   brought against the exact same Defendants does not change the outcome. See id.; Rubke, 
19   551 F.3d at 1161.                                                    
20        Plaintiffs’ cited authority does not compel an alternative conclusion. Knollenberg, 
21   152 F. App’x 674, In re Countrywide Financial Corp. Securities Litigation, 588 F. Supp. 
22   2d  1132  (C.D.  Cal.  2008)  (hereinafter  “In  re  Countrywide”),  and  Tsirekidze  v. 
23   Syntax-Brillian Corp., No. CV-07-02204-PHX-FJM, 2009 WL 275405 (D. Ariz. Feb. 4, 
24   2009), each predate the Ninth Circuit’s guidance in Rubke and In re Rigel. While the court 
25   in Boston Retirement System v. Uber Technologies, Inc., No. 19-cv-06361-RS, 2020 WL 
26   4569846 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 7, 2020), held the plaintiffs’ disclaimer sufficient to evade Rule 
27   9(b), there is no indication that the plaintiffs there relied on the exact same alleged false or 
28   misleading statements in its Sections 10(b) and 11 claims. See id. Similarly, in Flynn v. 
1   Sientra, Inc., No. CV 15-07548 SJO (RAOx), 2016 WL 3360676 (C.D. Cal. June 9, 2016), 
2   the  court  expressly  found  that  the  plaintiffs’  fraud  claims  were  based  on  “unique, 
3   particularized facts.” Id. at *17. Not so here. Accordingly, the Court applies Rule 9(b) to 
4   Plaintiffs’ Section 11 claims.

24             3.   Negative Causation                                    
25        Plaintiffs’ claims under Section 11 do not require proof of loss causation. Hildes v. 
26   Arthur Andersen LLP, 734 F.3d 854, 859 (9th Cir. 2013) (“[Plaintiffs] need only show a 
27   material misstatement or omission to establish [a] prima facie case.”). Defendants may 
28   avoid liability by establishing that the alleged losses “are not attributable to the alleged 
1   misrepresentations or omission in the registration statement.” Id. at 860. This affirmative 
2   defense is known as “negative causation.” Id.                        
3        A defendant raising the negative causation defense bears the burden of proof, and it 
4   is a “heavy burden.” Id. They “must show that the depreciation in value of a plaintiff’s 
5   stock resulted from factors other than the alleged material misstatement.” Id. (internal 
6   quotations  omitted).  Additionally,  “[b]ecause  an  analysis  of  causation  is  often 
7   fact-intensive, negative causation is generally established by a defendant on a motion for 
8   summary judgment or at trial.” In re Countrywide, 588 F. Supp. 2d at 1171. 
9        As analyzed above, the Court finds that none of the purported corrective disclosures 
10   cited by Plaintiffs in their briefs withstand scrutiny. Courts within the Ninth Circuit and 
11   elsewhere  have  found  negative  causation  established  where  the  defendants  have 
12   demonstrated  that  the  plaintiffs  failed  to  allege  a  corrective  disclosure  or  any  other 
13   indication of loss causation. See e.g., Brown v. Ambow Educ. Holding Ltd., No. CV 
14   12-5062 PSG (AJWx), 2014 WL 523166, at *16 (C.D. Cal. Feb. 6, 2014) (collecting cases). 
15   And while, in some instances, it may be appropriate to reserve the issue for a later time, 
16   the Court concludes that postponing the issue would serve no legitimate purpose. See id. at 
17   *14 (“While the loss causation analysis is fact intensive and often more appropriate at the 
18   summary judgment phases, courts in the Ninth Circuit routinely apply Rule 12(b)(6) when 
19   the face of the complaint demonstrates that the plaintiff cannot establish loss causation.”). 
20   Here, the Court finds that Defendants have established negative causation because they 
21   have  demonstrated  that  Plaintiffs  do  not  allege  a  corrective  disclosure  or  any  other 
22   indication of loss causation in their Consolidated Amended Complaint.  
23        For these reasons, the Court finds that Plaintiffs’ claims against Defendants brought 
24   pursuant to Section 11 fail.                                         
25        C.   Sections 15 and 20(a)                                      
26        A claim under Section 15 of the Securities Act is a derivative claim: it “require[s] 
27   [an] underlying primary violation[] of the securities laws.” See In re Rigel, 697 F.3d at 886; 
28                                                                        
1   see also 15 U.S.C. § 77o.                                            
2        Similarly,  Section  20(a)  of  the  Exchange  Act  “imposes  liability  on  certain 
3   controlling individuals . . . for violations of [S]ection 10(b) and its underlying regulations.” 
4   Prodanova v. H.C. Wainwright & Co., LLC, 993 F.3d 1097, 1113 (9th Cir. 2021) (internal 
5   marks and citation omitted). To state a claim of control person liability under Section 20(a), 
6   a plaintiff must demonstrate “a primary violation of federal securities law” and that “the 
7   defendant  exercised  actual  power  or  control  over  the  primary  violator.”  Zucco,  552 
8   F.3d at 990.                                                         
9        Because Plaintiffs fail to plead a primary violation of Sections 10(b) or 11, the 
10   Sections 15 and 20(a) control person claims necessarily fail.        
11   IV.   LEAVE TO AMEND                                                 
12        Plaintiffs “request leave to replead.” (Doc. 56 at 23 n.9; see also Doc. 55 at 38 n.17.) 
13   District courts “shall grant leave to amend freely ‘when justice so requires.’” Lopez v. 
14   Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1130 (9th Cir. 2000) (en banc) (quoting Fed. R. Civ. P. 15 (a)). 
15   Courts in the Ninth Circuit are to apply this policy “with extreme liberality.” Morongo 
16   Band of Mission Indians v. Rose, 893 F.2d 1074, 1079 (9th Cir. 1990). The Court, however, 
17   “may in its discretion deny leave to amend due to undue delay, bad faith or dilatory 
18   motive . . . , repeated failure to cure deficiencies . . . , undue prejudice to the opposing party 
19   by virtue of the allowance of the amendment, [and] futility of amendment.” Zucco, F.3d at 
20   1007. Absent a “strong showing of any of [these] factors, there exists a presumption under 
21   Rule 15(a) in favor of granting leave to amend.” Eminence Capital, LLC v. Aspeon, Inc., 
22   316 F.3d 1048, 1052 (9th Cir. 2003) (emphasis in original).          
23        It is not clear to the Court that any further amendment to Plaintiffs’ Consolidated 
24   Amended Complaint would be futile. See Eminence Capital, 316 F.3d at 1052 (reasoning 
25   that dismissal with prejudice and “without leave to amend is not appropriate unless it is 
26   clear on de novo review that the complaint could not be saved by amendment”). Thus, 
27   Plaintiffs will be granted leave to file a Second Consolidated Amended Complaint.

24             2.   Scienter                                              
25        To state a claim under Section 10(b), Plaintiffs must make a showing of scienter, 
26   i.e., an intent to defraud. See Ernst & Ernst v. Hochfelder,
425 U.S. 185, 193
 (1976) 
27   (explaining  that  scienter  refers  to  the  mental  state  embracing  an  “intent  to  deceive, 
28   manipulate, or defraud”). “Mere negligence—even head-scratching mistakes—does not 
1   amount to fraud.” Prodanova v. H.C. Wainwright & Co., LLC,
993 F.3d 1097
, 1103 
2   (9th Cir. 2021).                                                     
3        Rule  9(b),  moreover,  requires  a  plaintiff  to  “state  with  particularity  the 
4   circumstances constituting fraud.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b). In enacting the PSLRA, Congress 
5   extended Rule 9(b)’s particularity requirement to allegations of scienter. Therefore, to 
6   adequately plead scienter, a complaint must “state with particularity facts giving rise to a 
7   strong inference that the defendant acted with the required state of mind.” 15 U.S.C. 
8   § 78u-4(b)(2)(A). To support a strong inference of scienter, a complaint must allege that a 
9   defendant made false or misleading statements with an “intent to deceive, manipulate, or 
10   defraud,” or with deliberate recklessness. City of Dearborn Heights Act 345 Police & Fire 
11   Ret. Sys. v. Align Tech., Inc.,
856 F.3d 605, 619
 (9th Cir. 2017). “Deliberate recklessness 
12   is not mere recklessness.” Prodanova,
993 F.3d at 1106
 (internal marks and citation 
13   omitted) (emphasis in original). Rather, it is “an extreme departure from the standards of 
14   ordinary care . . . which presents a danger of misleading buyers or sellers that is [] known 
15   to the defendant or is so obvious that the actor must have been aware of it.”
Id.
 (emphasis 
16   in original).                                                        
17        These  standards  “present  no  small  hurdle  for  the  securities  fraud  plaintiff.” 
18   Schueneman v. Arena Pharms., Inc.,
840 F.3d 698, 705
 (9th Cir. 2016) (citation omitted); 
19   see also Nguyen v. Endologix, Inc.,
962 F.3d 405, 414
 (9th Cir. 2020) (“The PSLRA’s 
20   strong inference requirement has teeth. It is an exacting pleading obligation.”) (cleaned 
21   up). The Court must “engage in a comparative evaluation [and] . . . consider, not only 
22   inferences urged by the plaintiff . . . but also competing inferences rationally drawn from 
23   the facts alleged.” Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights Ltd.,
551 U.S. 308, 314
 (2007).  
24   A complaint will survive a motion to dismiss “only if a reasonable person would deem the 
25   inference of scienter cogent and at least as compelling as any opposing inference one could

.

26             3.   Loss Causation                                        
27        Even if Plaintiffs had adequately pleaded a strong inference of scienter, their Section 
28   10(b) claims against the Opendoor Defendants would still fail due to their failure to plead 
1   loss causation.                                                      
2        Section 10(b) requires that plaintiffs asserting securities fraud “must plead and 
3   ultimately prove that the defendant’s wrongful conduct caused the plaintiff’s injury.” In re 
4   BofI Holding, 977 F.3d at 789. In enacting the PSLRA, Congress codified the requirement 
5   that plaintiffs “shall have the burden of proving that the act or omission of the defendant 
6   alleged to violate [the law] caused the loss for  which the plaintiff seeks to recover 
7   damages.” 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(b)(4).                                   
8        “Typically, to establish loss causation, a plaintiff must show that the defendants’ 
9   alleged misstatements artificially inflated the price of stock and that, once the market 
10   learned of the deception, the value of the stock declined.” Irving Firemen’s Relief & Ret. 
11   Fund,
998 F.3d at 407
 (citing Nuveen Mun. High Income Opportunity Fund v. City of 
12   Alameda,  Cal.,
730 F.3d 1111, 1119-20
  (9th  Cir.  2013)).  This  is  known  as  the 
13   “fraud-on-the-market” theory. Nuveen,
730 F.3d at 1120
. To advance this theory, “the 
14   plaintiff must show that after purchasing her shares and before selling, the following 
15   occurred: (1) the truth became known, and (2) the revelation caused the fraud-induced 
16   inflation in the stock’s price to be reduced or eliminated.” In re BofI Holding, 977 F.3d at 
17   789 (internal marks omitted). “The most common way for plaintiffs to prove that ‘the truth 
18   became known’ is to identify one or more corrective disclosures.” Id. at 790 (citing 
19   Mineworkers’ Pension Scheme v. First Solar Inc.,
881 F.3d 750, 753-54
 (9th Cir. 2018) 
20   (per  curiam)).  Corrective  disclosures  occur  “when  ‘information  correcting  the 
21   misstatement or omission that is the basis for the action is disseminated to the market.’”
Id.
 
22   (quoting 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(e)(1)).                                   
23        While  determining  what  constitutes  a  corrective  disclosure  “has  proved  more 
24   challenging than might have been expected, a few basic ground rules can be sketched out.”

26   or a formal finding of fraud by a government agency.” Id. (citing Metzler,
540 F.3d at 27

28   knowledgeable third parties such as whistleblowers, analysts, or investigative reporters.”

Id.

2   defendant’s  fraud  in  one  fell  swoop;  the  true  facts  concealed  by  the  defendant’s

, 1210

411 F.3d 1006, 1027

2   2005) (quoting In re Stac Elecs. Sec. Litig.,
89 F.3d 1399, 1403-04

Id.
 A defendant is “liable for innocent

Id.
               
5        1.   Applicability of Rule 9(b)’s Heightened Pleading Standard  
6        Importantly, “the heightened pleading requirements of the PSLRA do not apply to 
7   Section 11 claims.” Rubke v. Capitol Bancorp Ltd.,
551 F.3d 1156, 1161
 (9th Cir. 2009). 
8   Nonetheless, “plaintiffs are required to allege their claims with increased particularity 
9   under Rule 9(b) if their complaint sounds in fraud.”
Id.
 (cleaned up). The Ninth Circuit has 
10   advised that where “a complaint employs the exact same factual allegations to allege 
11   violations of [S]ection 11 as it used to allege fraudulent conduct under [S]ection 10(b) of 
12   the Exchange Act, [the Court] can assume that it sounds in fraud.”
Id.
 Otherwise, the Court 
13   must consider “whether the complaint ‘allege[s] a unified course of fraudulent conduct’ 
14   and rel[ies] entirely on that course of conduct as the basis of a claim.”
Id.
 (quoting Vess v. 
15   Ciba-Geigy Corp. USA,
317 F.3d 1097, 1103-04
 (9th Cir. 2003)) (alterations in original). 
16   If it does, the claim sounds in fraud.
Id.
                           
17        The parties disagree over whether Rule 9(b) applies to Plaintiffs’ Section 11 claims. 
18   The Opendoor Defendants argue that it does because the claims sound in fraud. They argue 
19   that “although Plaintiffs expressly disclaim that their Section 11 claim sounds in fraud, this 
20   disclaimer is belied by their repeating of the exact same factual allegations used to support

22   in the Opendoor Defendants’ arguments. (Doc. 51 at 8-9; Doc. 62 at 7-9.)

24   [Consolidated  Amended]  Complaint  carefully  segregates  Plaintiffs’  negligence-based 
25   Securities Act claims from the fraud-based Exchange Act claims,” “the Securities Act 
26   claims expressly disclaim any allegations of fraud, fraudulent conduct, improper motive or 
27   any intentional or reckless misconduct,” and “the Securities Act and Exchange Act claims 
28   are distinct claims against different defendants.” (Doc. 56 at 13-14 (cleaned up).) 
1        The Court finds that Plaintiffs’ Section 11 claims sound in fraud because the exact 
2   same factual allegations underlie both Plaintiffs’ Sections 10(b) and 11 claims. (Compare 
3   Doc. 39 ¶¶ 62-84, 118-29, 166-82 with id. ¶¶ 401-60.) Specifically, Plaintiffs allege the

5   id. ¶¶ 402, 405, 407, 410, 412, 414.) Because “the [S]ection 11 claim . . . merely relies on 
6   the same alleged misrepresentations . . . that are central to Plaintiff[s]’ [S]ection 10(b) fraud

697 F.3d 869
, 885-86 
9   (9th Cir. 2012) (hereinafter “In re Rigel”).

11   Harmonic,  Inc.,
152 F. App’x 674, 684

13   In re Rigel,
697 F.3d at 885-86
. There is no magic pleading technique that transforms a

152 F. App’x at 684
; see 
15   also In re Rigel,
697 F.3d at 885-86

17
697 F.3d at 885-86

551 F.3d at 1161
.

152 F. App’x 674

24             3.   Negative Causation                                    
25        Plaintiffs’ claims under Section 11 do not require proof of loss causation. Hildes v. 
26   Arthur Andersen LLP,
734 F.3d 854, 859
 (9th Cir. 2013) (“[Plaintiffs] need only show a 
27   material misstatement or omission to establish [a] prima facie case.”). Defendants may 
28   avoid liability by establishing that the alleged losses “are not attributable to the alleged 
1   misrepresentations or omission in the registration statement.”
Id. at 860
. This affirmative 
2   defense is known as “negative causation.”
Id.
                        
3        A defendant raising the negative causation defense bears the burden of proof, and it 
4   is a “heavy burden.”
Id.
 They “must show that the depreciation in value of a plaintiff’s 
5   stock resulted from factors other than the alleged material misstatement.”
Id.
 (internal 
6   quotations  omitted).  Additionally,  “[b]ecause  an  analysis  of  causation  is  often 
7   fact-intensive, negative causation is generally established by a defendant on a motion for 
8   summary judgment or at trial.” In re Countrywide, 588 F. Supp. 2d at 1171. 
9        As analyzed above, the Court finds that none of the purported corrective disclosures 
10   cited by Plaintiffs in their briefs withstand scrutiny. Courts within the Ninth Circuit and 
11   elsewhere  have  found  negative  causation  established  where  the  defendants  have 
12   demonstrated  that  the  plaintiffs  failed  to  allege  a  corrective  disclosure  or  any  other 
13   indication of loss causation. See e.g., Brown v. Ambow Educ. Holding Ltd., No. CV 
14   12-5062 PSG (AJWx),
2014 WL 523166
, at *16 (C.D. Cal. Feb. 6, 2014) (collecting cases). 
15   And while, in some instances, it may be appropriate to reserve the issue for a later time, 
16   the Court concludes that postponing the issue would serve no legitimate purpose. See
id.
 at 
17   *14 (“While the loss causation analysis is fact intensive and often more appropriate at the 
18   summary judgment phases, courts in the Ninth Circuit routinely apply Rule 12(b)(6) when 
19   the face of the complaint demonstrates that the plaintiff cannot establish loss causation.”). 
20   Here, the Court finds that Defendants have established negative causation because they 
21   have  demonstrated  that  Plaintiffs  do  not  allege  a  corrective  disclosure  or  any  other 
22   indication of loss causation in their Consolidated Amended Complaint.  
23        For these reasons, the Court finds that Plaintiffs’ claims against Defendants brought 
24   pursuant to Section 11 fail.
